opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer starts with the fact that I'm a physicist by training, and physicists love a system they can actually poke at. For most of history, if you wanted to understand intelligence, your only examples were brains, and brains are extraordinarily hard to study. You can't freely open them up, you can't rewind them, you can't change one parameter and rerun the experiment a thousand times. You're mostly inferring from the outside.

With AI systems, for the first time we have something that does at least some of the things we associate with intelligence, like learning from data, generalizing, reasoning in a rough way, and we have complete access to it. Every weight, every activation, the whole training history. We can scale it up and watch what changes, or ablate pieces and see what breaks. That's the kind of setup where the tools of physics really shine: you look for regularities, like scaling laws, you build effective theories that ignore microscopic details and capture the behavior that matters, and you check them against experiment.

I'm not claiming a neural network is a brain. The substrate is different, the learning algorithm is almost certainly different. But I suspect some principles are universal, in the same sense that very different materials share the same behavior near a phase transition. If there are general principles about how a system extracts structure from data and builds useful representations, then studying the system we can fully inspect is probably the most direct way to find them. Then you can take those ideas back and ask whether the brain is doing something analogous.

So for me AI is partly an engineering project, and it's also a kind of model organism for intelligence, the fruit fly of thinking, if you like. That's what makes it so exciting scientifically.

r001.rationale: The response describes access to weights, activations, and training history, and says researchers can ablate parts to see what breaks. It does not clearly identify tracing humanlike behavior back to the code that implements it.

r002.rationale: The response calls AI a “model organism for intelligence” and compares it to “the fruit fly of thinking,” proposing that studying AI can reveal principles to investigate in the brain.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I come at this from physics, so my instinct is always to look for the simplest system that exhibits the phenomenon you care about. If you want to understand turbulence, you don't start with the atmosphere, you start with a pipe. And for a long time, intelligence didn't have anything like a pipe. You had the human brain, which is extraordinarily complicated, hard to measure, hard to perturb ethically, and basically one of a kind. So you were stuck doing a kind of observational science.

What's changed is that we now have artificial systems that clearly do something intelligence-like. They write, they reason a bit, they generalize. And unlike brains, we built them. We know every parameter, we know exactly what data went in, we can rerun the training with a different seed or a different dataset size and see what changes. That's an experimental handle that neuroscience and psychology have never really had.

Now, I want to be careful here. I don't think a transformer is a brain, and I don't think the mechanisms are going to map over one to one. But that's actually not what makes it useful. What's useful is that it gives you a second example. If you've only ever seen one instance of a thing, you can't tell which features are essential and which are accidents of how it happened to arise. With two instances, you can start to ask: what's common? What survives when you change the substrate entirely?

And a lot does seem to survive. You see scaling behavior, where capability improves in a lawful, predictable way with size and data. You see representations forming that look an awful lot like things people have found in cortex. You see learning dynamics with phases and transitions. When the same structure shows up in silicon and in biology, that's a hint that it isn't about the hardware at all, that it's about the statistics of the problem and the constraints of learning from finite experience. Those are the kinds of universal principles a physicist gets excited about.

So the short version is: AI gives us intelligence as a laboratory object for the first time. Even if the models end up being a poor model of us in the details, the act of taking them apart is forcing us to sharpen questions about intelligence in general that we've been asking vaguely for a century.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers know the models’ parameters and can experiment with training, but it does not identify tracing humanlike behavior to the code that implements it as a way to understand that behavior.

r002.rationale: The response presents AI as a second, experimentally tractable example of intelligence that can reveal which features are essential and help clarify principles of intelligence across biological and artificial systems.

astra-6.text:
I think AI gives us a way to turn questions about intelligence into things we can actually test. With humans, we see this extraordinary ability to learn, reason, and generalize, but we don’t have direct access to how all of that works. With an artificial system, we can control the training experience, change the architecture, and look at what happens as it learns.

That doesn’t mean a neural network is a faithful model of the brain. But if a relatively simple learning process produces abilities we thought required some very special machinery, that changes the questions we ask about ourselves. And the differences are informative, too: why does a human learn something from a few examples when a machine needs so many? AI gives us another system to compare against, and that makes the study of intelligence much more concrete.

r001.rationale: The response describes controlling and observing artificial systems, but does not identify tracing their implementing code as the way to understand intelligent behavior.

r002.rationale: It presents AI as a simpler system for comparing learning and reasoning abilities with humans, and says that comparison makes the study of intelligence more concrete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think building something is a powerful way to test whether you understand it. We can have theories about how people learn, reason, or use language, but turning those theories into a working system forces us to be precise. What information does it need? What does it learn from experience? Where does it fail?

That doesn’t mean an AI system necessarily works the way a human brain does. Different mechanisms can produce similar behavior. But those similarities and differences give us a way to sharpen our questions about human intelligence. If a system can do something we thought required a particular human ability, we have to reconsider what that task actually tells us.

r001.rationale: The response says building a working system forces precision, but does not identify tracing humanlike behavior to its implementing code as the way AI makes intelligent behavior understandable.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems’ similarities and differences can sharpen questions about human intelligence, but does not propose studying them as simplified examples of human capacities.
